subjects.summary: A ceramic roof, stair and platform make architecture portable. The Met proposes that this model once formed an incense-burner lid. Western Mexican offering traditions and a separately excavated shaft tomb help explain how people connected made objects, funerary places and social relationships, while leaving this model’s precise findspot and use unresolved.

sections.title: Making architecture portable
sections.text: Look at the roof, the space beneath it and the stair rising from the platform. A maker brought these parts together in a ceramic object only 17.8 centimeters high. The miniature emphasizes levels and an approach to the roofed space. It does not give a scale for a full-size building or preserve every wall, material and activity. The catalogue calls it a temple model, but it identifies no particular surviving building, maker or workshop. Describing what the clay represents is a first step toward asking what people did with it.

sections.title: A possible vessel component
sections.text: The museum suggests that the model may have served as an incense-burner lid. If so, architecture was made part of a vessel and its use, rather than a working prototype for builders. This interpretation connects form with an action that the photograph alone cannot recover. No associated burner body or residue result is supplied. Pillsbury compares ancient miniatures with several intentions and functions; a similar building shape need not mean a toy, an identical ritual or contact between the makers of distant objects.

sections.title: Preparing places and gifts
sections.text: In parts of western Mexico, people excavated underground funerary chambers reached by a vertical shaft. Preparing these places involved work on the ground as well as making and arranging offerings. INAH describes vessels, architectural models, stone and shell objects among regional deposits, with differences in chamber form and number. Pillsbury places western Mexican models within this offering tradition and discusses relationships between living people and the dead. Such contexts explain why a small building could carry social significance. They do not establish that this particular model came from a known tomb.

deeperReading.title: One excavated place supplies an association
deeperReading.text: Huitzilapa, in central Jalisco’s Magdalena basin, offers a different kind of evidence from a regional museum attribution. The excavators’ 1996 abstract describes an unlooted shaft tomb and radiocarbon dates clustering in the first century CE. The 2006 organic-study abstract discusses six interments in two chambers. These associations connect objects and people within a documented place. Only the exposed abstracts were consulted here; the complete excavation record and original dating tables were not read. Huitzilapa is a comparison, not the selected model’s newly discovered origin.

deeperReading.title: Materials reveal work with different levels of certainty
deeperReading.text: The organic-study authors examined burial materials with light and scanning electron microscopy. They report cotton and agave fibres and paper, while many presumed food offerings could be identified only as broad animal or plant categories. Such remains bring clothing, wrapping and the provision of gifts into the explanation. The authors interpret differences as evidence of status. Material identification and social meaning are different steps; neither supplies a complete menu, each participant’s intentions or a universal funerary belief.

subjects.question: What can a city plan reveal about collective life?
subjects.summary: Teotihuacan was made through public construction and the work of households. At Tlajinga, blade production, courtyards and drains connect modest residences to a larger urban system. Nearby platform buildings had different materials and activities. These remains explain practical organization and change while leaving the identities and exact powers of many decision makers uncertain.

sections.title: A city was built at different moments
sections.text: Teotihuacan’s great monuments and apartment compounds belong to different phases of urban life. Barnes places major monumental building around 100–250 CE and apartment development especially around 250–550. Rooms, courtyards and streets therefore need dates as well as positions on a plan. The city’s broad history continues into a period of reduced population after 600. A single drawing cannot make every building contemporary, and a later artifact cannot be fixed to the year 200 merely because it appears beside that view.

sections.title: A household could also make tools
sections.text: In the southern district of Tlajinga, excavators investigated parts of Compounds 17 and 18. Compound 17 preserves cores and byproducts from making obsidian blades, sharp cutting tools used widely in the city. Producing these useful goods helped residents obtain things they did not make themselves. The project interprets differences in skill as evidence of apprenticeship and work across generations. That gives production a household setting, although it does not identify an individual apprentice, their age, or the rules by which work was assigned.

sections.title: Shared spaces linked homes to the street
sections.text: Building materials varied: some walls used cut stone, others smaller stones, rubble or adobe. Courtyards provided space for gatherings and domestic ritual, while drains from Compounds 17 and 18 emptied toward the Street of the Dead. These connections made household life part of the city’s physical organization. Modest construction did not mean isolation: residents also obtained some greenstone, shell, mica and decorated pottery. Different kinds of access and material work could coexist within the same district.

sections.title: A neighborhood center had a changing role
sections.text: Across the street, elevated platform buildings used more elaborate surfaces and decoration. Recent research compares their floors, tools and pottery with nearby apartments. Greater domestic residues and grinding-tool densities in the apartments support different food-related activities. At Complex 2, earlier structures were covered with fill before raised buildings were constructed. Excavators interpret its later use as more civic-ceremonial, within the areas investigated. Such changes reveal organization at the neighborhood scale without supplying the names of its decision makers or proving that every household had equal power.

subjects.question: Does a widespread object mean one shared purpose?
subjects.summary: Bronze drums enter histories of making, depositing and reusing objects. A miniature, a group of bronze implements and a wooden-jar cover answer different questions. Selected Vietnamese contexts show that a repeated form could acquire local roles; wider circulation does not establish one purpose, people or polity.

sections.title: Begin with the object’s actual scale
sections.text: The selected bronze miniature stands 10.2 cm high. Four frogs sit near its decorated upper rim, above a body that flares toward the base. Its small size matters when considering handling and use: Ngọc Lũ, a different drum, is 63 cm high. The Met describes both Vietnam-made drums and works made locally elsewhere across mainland and island Southeast Asia. That wider history does not identify this miniature’s place of discovery or establish whether it sounded in a ceremony.

sections.title: Objects were gathered into particular groups
sections.text: At Mả Tre within Cổ Loa, a drum found in 1982 contained agricultural implements, weapons and other objects, including bronze scraps. The site record describes it as buried upside down. The association brings tools for different activities into one deposited group. It gives the drum a documented context beyond its decorated surface, although the account does not recover who assembled the group, why they deposited it, or how long the objects had been used.

sections.title: Wood, cloth and a drum belonged to another setting
sections.text: At waterlogged Phú Chánh, excavators recorded wooden containers, pottery and textile-related materials. In Pit 6, a drum was positioned over a wooden jar. Other deposits included wooden equipment later identified as parts of weaving apparatus, after comparison changed an earlier interpretation as elite equipment. Carving containers and working textiles thus enter the account alongside bronze. The excavator calls the pits presumed graves: no bones survived in the acid soil, so these objects cannot identify a particular buried person’s work or gender.

sections.title: Making leaves evidence beyond the finished drum
sections.text: At Luy Lâu, excavators found inner and outer mould fragments representing different drum parts, together with crucibles, furnace-related remains and slag. These remains connect shaped bronze to the preparation of moulds, heating metal and the disposal of workshop material. The 2024 preliminary account associates this evidence with third–sixth-century-CE material. This later production reference extends beyond the miniature’s case interval; it neither identifies its workshop nor supplies a recipe used for every drum.

deeperReading.title: A named place can have more than one recorded role
deeperReading.text: Ngọc Lũ is not a secure discovery coordinate simply because it names a drum. The museum’s 2013 account places discovery there and later ceremonial use at Như Trác. Its 2023 account instead describes discovery during embankment works at Như Trác and subsequent use at Ngọc Lũ communal house. Showing both locality references makes the disagreement inspectable. It does not create two ancient finds or prove a route. The later English date line is malformed and cannot supply a calendar chronology.

deeperReading.title: Material dates answer different questions
deeperReading.text: The official Phú Chánh treasure record assigns its drum to the second–first centuries BCE and reports a wood radiocarbon result. The 2008 excavation paper lists four different wood BP results for the site. These are not interchangeable dates for making every associated object. Similarly, Luy Lâu’s 2016 account distinguishes dating by drum style from dating the layer’s associated materials. Keeping those steps separate allows later discoveries to change an explanation without shortening the miniature’s inherited range.

deeperReading.title: Distribution needs local histories
deeperReading.text: A map point can orient a documented association while leaving movement unresolved. These selected Vietnamese contexts do not represent the complete mainland and island distribution described by the Met. Similar forms may involve movement of objects, skills or ideas and local manufacture. Establishing a particular route or political relationship requires additional evidence; the shared form alone cannot choose between those histories.

subjects.question: Whose account of power survives on a palace wall?
subjects.summary: At Kalhu, now Nimrud, making a royal palace joined skilled material work, protective imagery and claims about conquest and settlement. A later archive also preserves administrative commands concerning captives. These different sources explain how royal institutions represented power and sought practical results, while keeping the people subjected to those decisions distinct from the official voices that survive.

sections.title: Making a royal centre
sections.text: Ashurnasirpal II made Kalhu, now Nimrud, a royal capital during his reign of 883–859 BCE. His Northwest Palace gathered rooms and courtyards into a setting for royal business, ceremony and residence. Building such a place joined materials and skilled work: mud brick formed its walls, while large slabs of local gypsum lined selected interiors. Quarrying, moving, carving and painting those slabs made authority into a substantial environment that people could enter.

sections.title: Protection around the ruler
sections.text: The surviving panel shows a bird-headed winged figure wearing patterned clothing and holding a bucket. The museum interprets such figures as protective beings. Doorways and rooms made their placement consequential: protection and royal power were presented together as people moved through the building. The throne room also carried scenes of warfare and hunting, while protective imagery appeared widely elsewhere. The palace therefore offered more than a record of events; its makers arranged a particular account of power.

sections.title: The king claims a city
sections.text: Writing ran across many reliefs. In the recurring Standard Inscription, the king named divine supporters, victories and palace materials. He also claimed to have rebuilt Kalhu and settled there people taken from conquered territories. That passage connects the splendid building programme to coercive movement of people. It supplies the ruler’s account of settlement, rather than the voices of those moved. Neither a carved figure nor this text identifies the legal status of every quarry worker, carver or palace servant.

sections.title: Keeping the institution working
sections.text: The palace was also a place of storage, preparation and administration. Excavated rooms and finds help researchers identify these practical activities: Room ZZ contained an oven and cooking vessels, while other areas held stores and archives. These remains come from a building used and altered over generations. Their dates matter. A plan can locate rooms and show relationships between them, but a composite excavated plan cannot make every room or activity contemporary with Ashurnasirpal.

sections.title: Another official voice survives
sections.text: A later letter from the palace archive, assigned by its editors to about 732 BCE, orders officials to provision captives and care for sick people among them. It reveals responsibilities and threats inside imperial administration. The order does not prove that its recipients complied. This eighth-century record expands the reference context without changing this case’s ninth-century dates. Reading wall, plan and letter together exposes different institutional purposes; none gives everyone governed by Assyria an equal voice.

deeperReading.title: Read an arrangement, then ask about its date
deeperReading.text: A palace plan lets us ask how activities were placed in relation to one another. The published Northwest Palace drawing locates the throne room B, courtyards and southern service spaces. Robson’s account links Room ZZ with an oven and cooking vessels, and identifies northern areas with administration and storage. These functional readings combine architecture and finds; a room label is not an ancient sign naming its occupants. The drawing also includes later features. It should be read as a composite of excavated remains, with the north arrow and scale retained, rather than a snapshot of one reign. The modern museum arrangement creates another layer: gathering panels from different rooms helps visitors compare them, but changes their architectural relationships. That useful display should be distinguished from evidence of an intact ancient room.

deeperReading.title: An order is evidence of a system, not its successful outcome
deeperReading.text: The later letter names two officials and makes captives their responsibility. Its surviving text combines provision with a threat against neglect. That detail shows how the king sought to make subordinates answerable within a coercive institution. The words do not establish that food reached everyone, that sick people recovered or that those moved consented. Its damaged passages and the editors’ proposed date must travel with any excerpt. Comparing it with the Standard Inscription reveals a useful difference: a public royal claim celebrates achievement, while an administrative command seeks action. Both speak from positions of authority. People subjected to those decisions are present in their content, but their own accounts are absent from these selected sources.

subjects.question: What changes when a ruler speaks to people in different languages?
subjects.summary: Ashoka’s rule depended on people carrying, interpreting and acting on messages across regions. Rock and pillar inscriptions address moral conduct, officials and religious communities in different settings. They announce practical actions as well as ideals, but an announcement is not an inspection of its results. Reading selected edicts beside their places and audiences shows how royal government sought to work, and whose experiences still need other evidence.

sections.title: A message needed a local audience
sections.text: Neelis describes regional Prakrit inscriptions and Greek and Aramaic material at Kandahar. Language and script are separate choices. Neither proves that everyone nearby could read the message; hearing and explanation are further questions. The geographic distribution shows attention to different audiences. It does not outline every territory controlled by the Mauryas or trace one messenger’s journey.

sections.title: The announced actions were practical
sections.text: In Hultzsch’s English edition, Girnar Rock Edict II describes provision for people and cattle, planting useful herbs and digging wells and planting trees along roads. These are tasks requiring materials, people and continuing access, rather than an abstract slogan about kindness. Yet the royal statement alone does not identify every worker, demonstrate that every well was maintained or show how benefits were distributed. An account of implementation would need evidence from particular places and later use.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 3–4, Girnar II, sections A–D

sections.title: Officials were told how to exercise power
sections.text: Dhauli Separate Edict I addresses judicial officials at Tosali. The translated text asks for impartial treatment and warns about anger, haste, fatigue and other obstacles to good judgment. This gives a concrete mechanism for royal instruction: address the people making decisions and tell them how their work should change. It also preserves the king’s paternal authority over subjects. It is not a grant of equal political participation, a record of every judgment or proof that abusive treatment stopped.

sections.title: Conquest and moral instruction belong together
sections.text: Rock Edict XIII expresses remorse over Kalinga’s conquest. The resulting account should keep warfare and the king’s moral presentation visible together, rather than turn remorse into proof that power no longer involved coercion. Neelis distinguishes the broader moral and administrative program of dhamma from a complete statement of Buddhist doctrine. Ashoka patronized Buddhist institutions and also supported other religious communities. Different inscriptions and audiences offer a more useful history than treating every carved message as one identical manifesto.

deeperReading.title: The message at Dhauli is not the whole series

Those local sets substitute the Separate Edicts for XI–XIII. The map therefore does not put the well-known remorse passage from XIII onto the Dhauli rock. A place, a version and an individual passage must stay connected. Hultzsch’s editorial English also belongs to 1925; it is not the language that an ancient audience saw on the stone. Later discoveries at Kandahar need the separate modern source used here.

deeperReading.title: Instructions let us ask about reception
deeperReading.text: An order directed at officials can be unusually revealing about the difficulties a ruler wanted to address. A warning against hurry suggests an administrative concern, but it does not tell us how often decisions were rushed. The king’s claim to care for subjects is similarly different from a subject’s own account of treatment. To deepen this inquiry, seek regional archaeological evidence, inscriptions in their linguistic settings and accounts that can test access and enforcement. Later religious narratives should retain their own dates and purposes, rather than be inserted as eyewitness reports of the reign.

subjects.question: Can an excluded political voice still be present in a city’s public life?
subjects.summary: Athenian public life combined decision-making, religious activity, markets and the work of supplying households. Those activities did not give everyone the same political powers. A water jar, excavated places, a constitutional account and later legal research illuminate different parts of that history. Together they make it possible to study participation and exclusion without erasing the people whose work kept the city functioning.

sections.title: Start with the jar and its own date
sections.text: The Met hydria dates to about 510–500 BCE. Its front shows women with vessels at a fountain; combat appears on the shoulder. Two horizontal side handles helped lift a hydria, and a vertical back handle served dipping and pouring. The shape and painted work give concrete things to inspect. The scene is an artistic representation near the conventional transition to democracy, not a photograph of a fourth-century household or a label identifying each depicted person’s legal status.

sections.title: Water connected households with public space
sections.text: Fetching water meant obtaining a necessary household resource outside the house. Rotroff and Lamberton compare images with literary accounts and discuss free and enslaved women carrying water, shopping and selling goods. Wealth and status affected who performed burdensome tasks and whose household could assign them to someone else. This evidence complicates elite male prescriptions about keeping respectable women at home. A fountain or market could be publicly used while access, work and power remained unequal.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 7–11, fountain house and public space

sections.title: Formal participation required eligibility
sections.text: The late-fourth-century Constitution of the Athenians describes male enrollment in local civic communities, or demes, at eighteen, with scrutiny of age, free status and parentage. Its account of the Council and Assembly explains procedures by which eligible citizens governed. Women, resident foreigners and enslaved people did not acquire those political powers simply by living or working in the city. Civic descent, religious roles, property and the franchise are distinct questions; exclusion from the Assembly is not evidence that a person had no public presence.

sections.title: Institutions occupied a changing city
sections.text: The Agora held commercial, religious and administrative activities; the Pnyx was a meeting place for the Assembly. Their different functions help distinguish being in public space from holding formal decision-making power. Neither the jar nor one constitutional description covers the whole sixth-to-fourth-century window. The parentage law and its later reestablishment belong to particular phases. A useful comparison follows how rules, institutions and everyday tasks intersected over time, rather than treating Athens as an unchanging community of equal participants.

Her argument is an interpretation of selective legal evidence, not a count of successful claims or a complete social survey. Court speeches also have interested speakers and audiences. Set their purposes beside the constitutional account’s procedural description and the archaeological evidence of ordinary work; no single source preserves everyone’s experience.

subjects.question: How can a funerary object connect royal power, work and belief?
subjects.summary: Taharqo’s royal institutions joined temple building and service with skilled production and claims over people and materials. A granite shabti attributed to his reign, probably from Nuri, connects that practical work with elite expectations of labor after death. Royal inscriptions, excavated faience production and a museum object label explain different parts of the history.

sections.title: A kingdom supported through temples
sections.text: Taharqo ruled Egypt and Kush in the Nile valley, with his reign conventionally dated to about 690–664 BCE. At Kawa, in present-day Sudan, he commissioned a sandstone temple and a shrine for Amun. The shrine’s reliefs showed him presenting offerings and wearing royal headgear. The Ashmolean’s teaching account describes priests caring for the god’s statue: awakening it, clothing it and presenting food. A temple therefore connected royal display with repeated practical tasks. People had to supply materials, make and maintain sacred objects, and perform ceremonies. These activities helped present the king’s relationship with Amun as a source of legitimate power.

citations.locator: Information sheet pp. 1–3, especially “Why did he build the shrine?” and “What can you see on the shrine?”

sections.title: Organising people and skilled work
sections.text: Kawa’s inscriptions also make claims about how the work was organised. In a passage discussed by Aleksandra Hallmann, Taharqo says that he sent work crews, craftspeople and a construction overseer while he remained in Memphis. This is a king announcing his provision, rather than a surviving diary kept by the builders. Another temple inscription lists male and female servants among his gifts. Such wording places people within royal resource claims and makes compulsion a necessary question; it does not tell us every worker’s status, payment or experience.

sections.title: A workshop makes the connection tangible
sections.text: Excavations at another temple founded by Taharqo, Sanam, uncovered firing pits, mudbrick basins, beads and damaged products from making faience, a manufactured quartz-rich material with a glazed surface. A clay mould from inside the temple matches an uninscribed green faience shabti fragment from the workshop. The excavators interpret this seventh-century production as evidence that temple institutions helped organise goods for royal funerary use. It brings skilled making into the explanation of power. This faience evidence concerns a different material and archaeological context from the granite figure shown here; it does not locate this particular figure’s workshop.

sections.title: Work imagined beyond life
sections.text: The selected figure is the Met’s granite shabti of Taharqo, only 20.3 centimetres high, probably associated with his pyramid at Nuri. Shabtis were intended to answer demands for work after death. The Met’s separate Seti I example explains tasks such as cultivation, irrigation and moving sand. That earlier object supplies general context, not a translation of Taharqo’s inscription. Here, a named king was commemorated through an object concerned with service and labor. Its material, carved writing and royal identity connect skilled production with elite expectations of the afterlife, while leaving ordinary households’ beliefs outside what this object alone can establish.

An older model does not automatically make the object older, and borrowing an old text is not evidence that a figure was made after the king died. deeperReading.title: Images claim a place in political history
deeperReading.text: Hallmann examines Kawa scenes in which the king appears as a sphinx overcoming enemies. She argues that their artists used older Egyptian compositions but changed the clothing of the depicted Libyan families to make a contemporary political statement. The reliefs consequently give evidence for the way kingship was presented; they need comparison with other sources before describing a particular battle. Read this interpretation alongside the king’s account of crews and temple gifts: both made resources and people visible through a royal voice. They support a history of institutions while leaving the workers’ own accounts largely unheard.

subjects.question: Does an imperial standard mean everyone followed it in the same way?
subjects.summary: An imperial standard needed people, materials and repeated work to become ordinary practice. Qin measuring objects announced central authority, while excavated wooden records show officials processing grain, reports and responsibilities in a conquered region. These sources let us compare what a government required with how an office worked. They preserve both coordination and constraint without making every official, worker or household identical.

sections.title: A common rule travelled on different devices
sections.text: A balance weight compares mass; a capacity measure holds volume. Either could carry an imperial decree while doing a different job. The Palace Museum dates its measure’s decree to the First Emperor’s 26th year, 221 BCE. The text announces conquest, imperial title and common standards, with peace as a royal claim. An inscribed decree did not prove accuracy in every transaction.

sections.title: A local office had to make records usable
sections.text: At Liye, excavated wood documents are associated with Qianling county administration and date mainly to 222–208 BCE. Officials wrote, received and annotated records. Staack compares actual tablets with prescriptions about size and writing layout, and studies tallies used when grain was issued. Reliable recording required the relevant facts to remain identifiable even when their arrangement varied. This was practical work: preparing writing surfaces, recording responsibility and keeping information available for another official to process or check.

sections.title: Making the writing surface was work too
sections.text: The paper connects the collection and preparation of wood with legal provisions and a fragment recording a person cutting tablets. It suggests that some stationery could have been made by assigned convict labor. That proposal matters because an archive depended on more people than the named scribes. The fragment does not identify the maker of every surviving tablet, and the labor arrangement remains a qualified reconstruction. Officials’ choices about materials and time should therefore be read alongside the unequal power that organized work.

sections.title: Uniformity had practical limits
sections.text: Lengths and required information were more consistent than some widths or layouts. Staack proposes practical reasons: compatible documents were easier to handle, while using narrower wood or more writing could save resources. These are explanations tested against a local archive, not proof that every departure was resistance or every office enjoyed the same freedom. Even fines did not guarantee identical documents. The contrast between prescribed form and observed practice makes standardization a historical process that needs investigation.

deeperReading.title: The comparison uses sources with different histories
deeperReading.text: The Liye records come from excavation; the Yuelu Academy manuscripts used for some prescribed formats were not archaeologically excavated. Staack explicitly says their exact provenance is unclear. Their contents and comparison with excavated material inform his argument, but they must not acquire a secure Liye findspot by being discussed beside that archive. The regional map locates the capital, Liye and the royal mausoleum; it does not mark Yuelu Academy as an ancient source location. A next inquiry should examine the relevant legal manuscripts and archaeological publications in greater detail.

deeperReading.title: One archive gives a local test, not a census
deeperReading.text: The study’s measured subsets depend on preservation and on what had been published with usable photographs. The differences it finds cannot be projected automatically to every Qin county. Even a named scribe’s preferred arrangement does not reveal all of that person’s training or choices. The author considers shortages of qualified staff and differing backgrounds as possible explanations. Following those questions requires additional archives and labor evidence, including people whose work produced records but who did not write an account of their own. Qin’s short imperial interval is also distinct from the longer history of the state and its projects.

packs.title: States, ideas and everyday voices
packs.question: How did power, techniques and systems of thought change across different regions?
packs.orientation: Different materials preserve different voices. Royal texts, ritual objects, household work and portable images make an uneven archive. Compare the purposes and audiences of those records while keeping each region’s chronology distinct.
packs.geography: Move from Mesopotamia to South Asia, Athens and the Nile, then across Andean and island worlds. These are comparisons; no connecting line is inferred from contemporaneity.
packs.limits: Selected contexts offer depth rather than a catalogue of all empires or philosophies. Achaemenid, Greek, Indian and Chinese intellectual histories extend well beyond these cases.

Americas.reason: Chavín textile, Olmec and Colima material histories; not all American regions.

Africa.reason: Taharqo now has temple, production and funerary-labor explanation with a distinct phased context, original figure, inspected workshop photographs and local source-qualified references. Kerma offers a separately dated comparative bridge, not an unbroken polity or a complete African framework.

Europe.reason: Expanded Athenian account separates Archaic image, changing civic eligibility, public work and later constitutional description. Other Greek and European histories remain outside this bounded set.

West/Central Asia.reason: Nimrud now pairs royal imagery with a primary settlement claim, a later captive-provision letter and a licensed composite palace plan. These distinct sources deepen work and authority without completing Assyrian social or regional history.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Ashoka account distinguishes regional versions, audiences, practical instructions and unmeasured outcomes within a separate Mauryan frame. Wider South Asian coverage remains selective.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Qin account separates measuring devices, prescriptions, excavated Liye practice and their distinct dates. Broader Chinese institutions, households and intellectual histories remain limited.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Dong Son material and Lapita cultural traditions with uncertain functions and distinct dates.

investigations.title: Rules, messages and public work
investigations.question: Who carried a rule into everyday life?
investigations.orientation: Compare Qin administrative work, Ashoka’s regional messages and Athenian public life in thematic order. These different places and dates are not one political ladder, a travel itinerary or evidence of contact.
investigations.geography: Locate a capital and a county archive, separate regional inscriptions, and Athenian public places. The maps are approximate locators with no connecting transmission route or reconstructed borders.
investigations.limits: Three expanded cases within a wider selective chapter. Qin legal provenance, regional reception and diverse Athenian work/status histories remain open; this does not complete global first-millennium BCE coverage.

investigations.title: Makers, supplies and royal claims
investigations.question: Who made and supplied things for powerful places?
investigations.orientation: Compare a carefully finished vessel, a palace environment and royal funerary objects. Each place depended on materials, skills and provision, but the evidence gives different views of work and authority. This thematic inquiry crosses separate centuries and institutions; it is not a journey, a single tradition of kingship or proof of contact between these particular cases.
investigations.geography: A Nubian capital and the beaker’s Egyptian findspot, selected Assyrian royal centres and separate Nuri/Sanam settings. Thematic comparison across different times; no connecting route or reconstructed border.
investigations.limits: Three bounded expansions preserve their case, reference, object and source dates. A composite small-source palace plan, mediated royal translations, the later archive letter and broad workshop chronology retain their limits. Wider labor histories and independent/human acceptance remain open.

evidence.prompt: Which comparison respects both institutions and ordinary work?

options.text: Records and objects reveal different tasks and powers; announcements, local practice and political eligibility require separate evidence.

options.text: Publishing a rule proves that every person experienced its promised result.

phases.label: c. 268–232 BCE
phases.title: The preserved reign convention
phases.text: The original dossier keeps Neelis’s dates. Inscriptions use relative regnal dates and do not all belong to one calendar year.

phases.title: Kalinga in a royal account
phases.text: This approximate viewing year derives from the retained reign convention. Edict XIII expresses remorse; Dhauli’s local set has different passages.

phases.title: Read particular messages
phases.text: Girnar II, Dhauli Separate I and Kandahar language evidence have separate settings. This anchor does not assign them all an exact issue date of 250 BCE.

phases.label: Around 185 BCE
phases.title: A later political transition
phases.text: Neelis describes the overthrow of the last Mauryan ruler while noting differing succession traditions. It is not the endpoint of the life of Ashoka’s inscriptions.

contexts.title: Athens: changing civic rules and public work

interval.label: Sixth–fourth centuries BCE: selected civic/work orientation
interval.note: Matches the analytical case window while separating the vase, changing eligibility rules and later procedural account. Neither boundary is the lifespan of Athens or democracy.

contexts.summary: The Archaic vase, fifth-century rules and fourth-century institutional description are different evidence within a broad teaching window.

phases.label: c. 510–500 BCE
phases.title: The selected water jar
phases.text: The Met vessel’s approximate date straddles a political transition; its scene is not an image of the later constitution.

phases.label: Around 508 BCE: conventional marker
phases.title: An institutional transition
phases.text: The Agora authors use this conventional democracy marker to distinguish their earlier vase from later texts. Institutions continued to change.

phases.label: 451/0 BCE
phases.title: A rule about civic descent
phases.text: Forsdyke dates the two-parent citizenship rule here. Female civic descent and male formal participation must not be collapsed into one role.

phases.label: 403 BCE
phases.title: A rule reestablished
phases.text: Forsdyke describes the parentage law’s reestablishment after interruption. The same eligibility rule was not simply unchanged across the whole case.

phases.label: Around 330 BCE
phases.title: The later procedural account
phases.text: The Constitution of the Athenians describes institutions of its own period while also narrating earlier changes. This is not the date of the selected jar.

contexts.title: Kushite and Egyptian power: temples, skilled work and royal claims

interval.label: c. 747–656 BCE: selected Dynasty 25 orientation
interval.note: Uses the 2026 Sanam article’s approximate Dynasty 25 frame, not the whole history of Kush or a continuous unchanged state. The retained case remains Taharqo’s c. 690–664 BCE reign. Kawa’s c. 680 BCE temple/shrine, individual shabti dates and the broadly dated Sanam workshop answer different questions. The workshop is not assigned an exact year or wholly to this reign; its ceramic discussion includes broader seventh–sixth-century parallels beyond this frame.

contexts.summary: Kushite rulers linked power in Egypt and Nubia with temple building, ritual service and the organisation of people and materials. Royal inscriptions, surviving objects and excavated production remains reveal different parts of those institutions.

contexts.title: Chavín: a highland centre and portable images

interval.label: Selected source frames, c.1500–200 BCE
interval.note: An orientation spanning differing centre/tradition conventions and the selected later textile, not one state’s lifespan. UNESCO’s Description gives 1500–300 BCE, its Brief Synthesis 15th–5th centuries BCE; the older Met chronology labels highland Chavín 1000–500 BCE. Neither replaces the complete unchanged 400–200 BCE object case. Phase dates below are attributed approximate points, not a newly modeled building sequence.

contexts.summary: Stone buildings, galleries and carved images made Chavín de Huántar a highland ceremonial centre. Portable objects support comparisons across media and places, while each object keeps its own date and provenance.

phases.label: Around 950 BCE in the Met’s 2004 chronology
phases.title: A carved image within the centre
phases.text: The museum places the Lanzón’s erection within the temple around this time. This is its approximate reference date, not a date for the textile.

phases.label: Around 850 BCE in the Met’s 2004 chronology
phases.title: Pilgrimage and specialist making
phases.text: Its account describes pilgrims and resident artisans producing several media. It does not identify the makers of this surviving fragment.

phases.label: Around 500 BCE in the Met’s 2004 chronology
phases.title: A changing monumental setting
phases.text: The museum describes declining Chavín power and changes at northern centres. Its convention is not proof that all related images or communities ended together.

phases.label: Fourth–third centuries BCE: the selected catalogue range
phases.title: This fragment has its own date
phases.text: The current catalogue assigns this cloth a later range. It does not locate its production at the highland centre or document a journey from there.

contexts.title: Teotihuacan: building a city and organizing neighborhood work

interval.label: c.100 BCE–650 CE: selected urban and neighborhood reference
interval.note: Selected teaching frame, not a lifespan or uniform polity. The case remains c.100 BCE–800 CE. The 650 edge lies within Barnes’s reduced-population period (600–800), not a collapse/abandonment date. Monuments, neighborhoods, samples and mask keep separate dates.

contexts.summary: Monuments and apartments developed at different times. Household production, shared spaces and changing construction explain urban organization without supplying a recovered list of rulers.

phases.label: Around 100 BCE: broad city chronology begins
phases.title: A broad frame is not the date of every building
phases.text: Barnes uses approximately 100 BCE–800 CE for Teotihuacan. This selected reference begins with that broad convention; it does not assign the later apartments or surviving mask to the first year.

phases.label: Around 100–250 CE: major monumental building
phases.title: Monuments and streets organize public space
phases.text: Barnes places major monumental construction in this interval. The orderly layout allows questions about coordination, but a single original master plan remains one interpretation rather than a demonstrated construction schedule.

phases.title: Household space becomes central to the urban account
phases.text: Barnes’s broad apartment-building range differs in scale from the Tlajinga report’s local transition to dense apartment occupation around the mid-third century. phases.title: A changed center does not identify its destroyers
phases.text: Barnes reports burning by unidentified people around this time. The event does not by itself establish its cause, the people responsible, or an immediate end to life in every neighborhood.

phases.label: After 600 CE: reduced population within a longer history
phases.title: Occupation continues beyond the main monumental phase
phases.text: Barnes describes markedly reduced population during 600–800 CE. The selected reference stops at 650 within that broader interval; the complete case continues to 800. Neither endpoint means that a people disappeared.

contexts.title: Đông Sơn traditions: selected find, use and production contexts

interval.label: c.700 BCE–600 CE: selected traditions and later production evidence
interval.note: Source-qualified teaching frame, not one continuous polity or universal drum chronology. The 2014 museum archaeological-culture scheme ends in the first/second centuries CE; later Luy Lâu production has a separate third–sixth-century interpretation. The complete miniature case stays c.500 BCE–300 CE, including its original note and precision. Later manufacture does not extend or redetermine that case.

contexts.summary: A shared bronze form enters different local settings. Find associations, later uses and production remains help distinguish those histories without drawing one state or a demonstrated movement route.

phases.label: Seventh–sixth centuries BCE: museum early-stage convention
phases.title: A broad archaeological frame precedes the miniature’s range
phases.text: The 2014 museum account identifies an early stage in varied upland, midland and delta settings. This attributed convention supplies orientation; it neither establishes a precise founding year nor dates the selected miniature to this stage.

phases.label: Fifth–third centuries BCE: museum middle-stage convention
phases.title: Regional settings and particular objects need separate dates
phases.text: The museum describes an extension into river and delta settings during its middle stage. Its broad scheme does not override the separate c.third–second-century-BCE date assigned to Ngọc Lũ in the 2013 object record, or the selected miniature’s wider catalogue interval.

phases.label: Second/first centuries BCE–first/second CE: museum late convention
phases.title: Different deposits supply local histories
phases.text: The source’s late-stage wording overlaps centuries rather than fixing one transition year. Phú Chánh’s official drum date and its wood results are different kinds of evidence; the excavation report calls the site about 2,000 years old. These conventions do not establish an exact shared year of use.

phases.label: Third–sixth centuries CE: later Luy Lâu production evidence
phases.title: Manufacture has a later reference of its own
phases.text: The 2024 preliminary field account associates mould and casting discard with Six Dynasties material. This later production interpretation extends beyond the case endpoint 300. The 2016 report separately distinguished typological dating from an approximately fourth-century associated layer. Neither identifies the Met miniature’s workshop.

contexts.title: Western Mexico: architecture, offerings and regional communities

interval.label: c. 300 BCE–400 CE: selected western Mexican funerary context
interval.note: Uses López Mestas’s 2026 Late Preclassic/Early Classic orientation, not the lifespan or borders of one Colima state. The selected model’s complete case remains 200 BCE–200 CE; its 2015 essay caption ends at 300 CE. Regional shaft-tomb conventions, an excavated first-century-CE Huitzilapa context and the undated creation of modern photographs answer different questions. The endpoint does not end every western Mexican funerary practice.

contexts.summary: People made architectural miniatures and prepared funerary places within varied western Mexican communities. A possible vessel lid, regional offering traditions and a documented excavation reveal different parts of that work.

phases.label: Around 300 BCE: beginning of the selected regional frame
phases.title: Shared mortuary forms did not require one state
phases.text: López Mestas describes western Mexican communities through a 300 BCE–400 CE orientation. Her account connects elaborate mortuary practices with different styles and autonomous villages or small chiefdoms. This is a regional interpretation of social relationships, not a founding date, common constitution or political border for everyone called Colima.

phases.label: 200 BCE–200 CE: the selected model’s catalogue range
phases.title: An object carries its own dating question
phases.text: The current Met record attributes this ceramic model to Colima and gives a broad 200 BCE–200 CE range. The date does not identify its maker, excavated tomb or precise year of manufacture. Roof, stair and platform can be observed in the supplied photograph while the proposed incense-burner-lid function remains an interpretation.

phases.label: First century CE: the separately excavated Huitzilapa tomb
phases.title: An excavation supplies an association
phases.text: The 1996 excavators report radiocarbon clustering in the first century CE at Huitzilapa, in central Jalisco. The 2006 organic-study abstract reports an averaged/calibrated date around 74 CE through that earlier study and describes six interments in two chambers. These are site-specific findings; the original laboratory tables were not consulted, and no object route or Huitzilapa origin is assigned to the Colima model.

phases.label: 200 CE and 300 CE: two published endpoints for the same model
phases.title: Keep a discrepancy visible
phases.text: The current catalogue ends the selected model’s range at 200 CE. The opening caption in Pillsbury’s 6 November 2015 essay ends it at 300 CE. This atlas retains the current catalogue interval and records the older alternative. Neither endpoint dates the end of a people or all shaft-tomb offerings.

phases.label: Around 400 CE: end of this selected regional orientation
phases.title: A teaching frame is not a universal ending
phases.text: The selected reference follows the 2026 essay’s regional endpoint. The INAH Colima account has its own wider shaft-tomb orientation and a local Comala convention of 200–400 CE. These differing scopes should remain identified, rather than being merged into a single rise-and-fall story or used to redate the museum object.

orientations.title: Ceremonial places and the histories of particular objects
orientations.question: How do we connect a portable image to a place without inventing its findspot?

summary.title: Chavín and Gulf Coast centres
summary.text: Chavín’s galleries, plazas and carved imagery offer one Andean ceremonial setting. San Lorenzo and La Venta offer distinct Gulf Coast histories of earth building and offerings. Comparing them asks how objects and built spaces shaped collective activity, without proposing one American religion or a connection demonstrated by resemblance alone.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: galleries, plazas and imagery

sections.title: An object travels with a different record
sections.text: The selected Chavín-style textile is a museum object with its own attribution and date. It is not automatically an excavated furnishing from the highland ceremonial centre. Likewise, a regional ceramic attribution does not place the selected Olmec figure in a known San Lorenzo household. Object catalogues and site histories must be linked with evidence, not just a shared label.

sections.title: A coastal setting at the later date
sections.text: For around 300 BCE, the Met’s Andean chronology describes Paracas Peninsula burials wrapped in layers of cloth and embroidered textiles. This is a coastal funerary setting with its own evidence. It supplies a dated comparison without extending the Chavín centre’s disputed endpoint or assigning the selected museum textile to a Paracas burial.

citations.locator: Key Events c300 BCE: funerary bundles

sections.title: Different endpoints change a snapshot
sections.text: UNESCO’s Chavín Description uses 1500–300 BCE, while its Brief synthesis gives the fifteenth through fifth centuries BCE. The discrepancy remains visible. The Gulf Coast account describes changes in prominent centres and continuing production elsewhere. Neither account supports the disappearance of every community at a single boundary.

orientations.perspectives: Ceremonial architecture and collected objects favour durable, selected remains. The people who made textiles, carried materials or maintained spaces are not represented by a complete set of personal accounts.
orientations.scope: Two named regional settings, with later Colima as a separate reading destination. The Chavín date conflict is unresolved; a broad cultural label cannot settle the chronology of every building.

activity.prompt: A caption places the museum textile inside Chavín’s temple in 300 BCE. Identify the two independent evidence checks that caption needs.
activity.response: Check excavation provenance before assigning the textile to the temple, and check its own date against the site’s conflicting chronology. Stylistic similarity alone supplies neither a findspot nor a precise year.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE, the museum chronology describes textile-wrapped burials on the Paracas Peninsula. This coastal setting supplies a dated comparison. Chavín’s conflicting summary endpoints remain unresolved; the selected museum textile is not assigned to a Paracas burial, and the later Colima case is not backdated.

orientations.title: Kushite institutions from Kawa to the Meroe region
orientations.question: How can temples, workshops and burial places reveal changes in royal organization?

summary.title: Several centres, separate histories
summary.text: Taharqo’s temple projects at Kawa and Sanam belong to an earlier Kushite royal setting. Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat es-Sufra provide a broader view of urban, religious and productive spaces. Their remains span many centuries and should not be collapsed into one ruler’s reign.

sections.title: Royal claims and working materials
sections.text: Kawa’s inscriptions claim arrangements for craftspeople and construction. Those are royal statements about work, not the workers’ own testimony. The later Meroe-region evidence includes production and water installations as well as temples and tombs, widening the questions beyond the image of a king alone.

sections.title: A change of burial centre is not a single population move
sections.text: UNESCO places most royal burials at Meroe from the third century BCE onward. That transition comes long after Taharqo’s reign. It helps orient a change in royal practice, but does not date every monument or imply that all households moved at once.

orientations.perspectives: Monuments and royal inscriptions foreground rulers. Workshops and water systems make other work visible, while leaving individual obligations and experiences incompletely recorded.
orientations.scope: Selected Nile and Kushite centres. No claim that all surviving Meroe-region monuments already existed in 300 BCE; the earlier shabti retains its own date and probable provenance.

activity.prompt: Explain why a royal inscription and an excavated workshop might support different statements about a building project.
activity.response: An inscription records what a ruler claimed to organize. Workshop remains support particular production activities. Use both while keeping the royal voice, archaeological interpretation and missing workers’ testimony distinct.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE marks the approach to the third-century BCE shift toward most royal burials at Meroe in UNESCO’s account. It is a broad transition marker, not an exact relocation event. Taharqo’s seventh-century BCE objects are earlier comparisons.

orientations.title: Public work and power in changing Greek settings
orientations.question: Is using public space the same as having a share in government?

summary.title: Athens and the later Hellenistic world
summary.text: Athenian water carrying brings household work into public space. Formal civic participation followed narrower rules. Later Hellenistic kingdoms and alliances place those questions within changing political settings, rather than extending one version of Athenian democracy across all Greek communities.

sections.title: Necessary work and political eligibility differ
sections.text: The hydria’s fountain scene can prompt questions about obtaining water. Literary and archaeological interpretation includes both free and enslaved women in public activity. The constitutional account’s male civic enrollment rules answer a different question: who could qualify for particular political roles.

sections.title: Patronage shifts with political settings
sections.text: After Alexander’s death in 323 BCE, successor rulers and Greek alliances shaped a different political landscape. Royal commissions supported buildings, sculpture and luxury production. Later, Rome became another centre employing Greek artists. These changes in patrons do not establish an identical experience for every craft worker.

citations.locator: Opening chronology; patronage; first-century BCE Rome

orientations.perspectives: The evidence separates people doing essential work from the narrower categories represented in political institutions. Images and official descriptions do not recover every excluded person’s experience.
orientations.scope: Athens is the close local inquiry; Hellenistic kingdoms and later Rome are dated comparisons. The sixth-century BCE jar is not a direct view of public life in 300 BCE.

activity.prompt: Give one reason a person might be visible at a public fountain but absent from a list of eligible political participants.
activity.response: Public work and residence do not by themselves establish the citizenship, status, age or gender eligibility described for particular institutions. A strong response distinguishes the image’s subject from the constitutional rule.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE falls after Alexander’s death and within the emerging Hellenistic political setting. Earlier Athenian objects and institutional descriptions offer comparisons, not proof that every Greek city retained the same arrangements at this date.

orientations.title: Royal centres and the work of governing across distance
orientations.question: How do buildings and images present power differently from administrative arrangements?

summary.title: Nimrud, Susa and Persepolis
summary.text: Nimrud’s palace reliefs present an Assyrian royal setting. Later Achaemenid building at Susa and Persepolis presents another imperial history. Their images help investigate how rulers represented power, while roads, governors and palace work raise practical questions about maintaining institutions.

citations.locator: Darius: roads, satraps and building projects

sections.title: An image of agreement is a claim
sections.text: At Persepolis, reliefs show people from different parts of the empire approaching or supporting the king. The arrangement presents imperial order. It cannot establish that every represented community agreed with the ruler or that obligations were experienced equally.

citations.locator: Persepolis reliefs and the impression of harmony

sections.title: Successor kingdoms need a new date frame
sections.text: Alexander’s conquest ended Achaemenid rule; after his death, successor kingdoms emerged, including the Seleucids in the Near East. The 300 BCE setting therefore cannot be represented simply by extending Ashurnasirpal II’s Nimrud or the Achaemenid court into the future.

orientations.perspectives: Royal monuments privilege the court’s desired image. Labour, tribute and administration involved people whose perspectives are only partly recoverable through those monuments.
orientations.scope: Selected royal centres and a successor-era orientation, not a complete West/Central Asian history. Similar palace imagery does not prove identical institutions or unbroken dynastic continuity.

activity.prompt: A relief depicts orderly tribute bearers. Write one observation and one claim that the relief cannot establish on its own.
activity.response: Observe the represented arrangement and figures. Do not treat the image as evidence of universal consent or equal obligations; those require other records and perspectives.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE belongs to the successor-kingdom setting after Alexander, including Seleucid power in the Near East. The Assyrian and Achaemenid palace readings are earlier institutional comparisons, not courts still ruling at this date.

orientations.title: Mauryan government before and during Ashoka
orientations.question: How does an official message differ from evidence that its instructions were followed?

summary.title: Pataliputra and audiences farther away
summary.text: Candragupta Maurya established rule from Pataliputra before Ashoka’s reign. Later inscriptions carried Ashoka’s policies to differently situated audiences, including Greek and Aramaic material at Kandahar. A capital, a message and its recipients are related but distinct parts of government.

citations.locator: Opening dynastic history; languages and inscriptions

sections.title: Messages needed language, materials and people
sections.text: Writing in different languages made official messages available in different settings. It did not mean that everyone could read them or that officials carried out every instruction. The linked edicts let readers inspect specific announced actions and compare royal ideals with the practical problem of implementation.

citations.locator: Girnar II, printed pp3–4; Dhauli Separate I, pp95–97

sections.title: Do not backdate the later ruler
sections.text: The university account places Candragupta’s transfer of power to Bindusara around 297–298 BCE and Ashoka’s reign around 268–232 BCE. The 300 BCE snapshot therefore precedes Ashoka’s inscriptions. Later evidence can illuminate a developing institution without becoming contemporary evidence for its earlier phase.

orientations.perspectives: Royal proclamations preserve the ruler’s chosen presentation. Recipients, officials and communities could have different experiences that the inscription itself does not settle.
orientations.scope: A justified institutional focus connecting a capital and differently addressed borderland messages. Not all South Asian communities were governed or addressed in the same way; later religious traditions remain distinct from contemporary inscriptions.

activity.prompt: An edict announces wells along roads. What is the difference between proving the announcement and proving its full implementation?
activity.response: The inscription supports that the ruler announced the policy. Dating and examining wells, administrative records and local evidence would be needed to assess where and how it was implemented.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE belongs to the early Mauryan setting under Candragupta, shortly before the source’s approximate transfer to Bindusara. Ashoka’s later inscriptions are a next reading, not evidence already issued at this snapshot date.

citations.locator: Opening paragraphs: succession c297–298 BCE; Ashoka c268–232 BCE

orientations.title: From competing states to imperial administration
orientations.question: What changes when rules and records must work across a larger territory?

summary.title: Qin, Chu and later imperial centres
summary.text: The Warring States frame includes competing polities rather than a single Qin empire. Chu’s lacquer and silk-painting evidence adds a distinct setting to the later Qin administrative inquiry. Court histories, craft objects and local records each expose different activities.

citations.locator: Timeline; 770 BCE and c400–200 BCE entries

sections.title: Common rules required practical handling
sections.text: The later Qin inquiry compares devices for measuring different quantities and wood documents used in county administration. The Liye records show that applying common requirements still involved choices about materials, layout and handling. A decree and its local paperwork need to be studied together.

sections.title: The empire follows the snapshot
sections.text: The museum’s Warring States convention runs from 475 to 221 BCE; imperial Qin follows in 221–206 BCE. Western Han then developed its capital at Chang’an. These changes do not make the later documents, tombs or capital features contemporary with 300 BCE.

orientations.perspectives: Administrative documents preserve tasks and categories useful to officials. Craft and material choices reveal other work, while leaving many workers’ own accounts unrecorded.
orientations.scope: Selected Chinese state and administrative settings, not all East Asia. The museum chronology’s inconsistent Qin Key Events heading is not adopted; its timeline and separate Qin essay establish the imperial dates.

activity.prompt: Explain why a later imperial measuring device cannot demonstrate that all states used one system in 300 BCE.
activity.response: Its date belongs to the later imperial frame. Establishing earlier uniformity would require contemporary evidence across the separate states, not a backward projection from an imperial decree.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE lies within the Warring States period, before imperial Qin. Chu and Qin provide distinct political settings; the later standardization and Liye paperwork are comparisons across a transition, not documents from this selected year.

orientations.title: Bronze deposits and changing island pottery traditions
orientations.question: Why does a change in objects not automatically mean the disappearance of a people?

summary.title: Vietnamese contexts and Tongan sequences
summary.text: Đông Sơn-associated drums occur in different kinds of deposits. Tonga’s earlier decorated pottery and later plainware provide a separate island history. Comparing them makes the relationship between an object category, a dated deposit and a community an explicit question.

sections.title: Find context changes the question
sections.text: A drum containing tools at Cổ Loa and a drum associated with a wooden container at Phú Chánh do not provide identical evidence of use. The small museum drum has another collection history. Their dates and contexts must be established independently before drawing conclusions about shared ritual or ordinary work.

sections.title: A ceramic endpoint is not a human endpoint
sections.text: The Tongan study argues that ceramic manufacture had ceased by about 400 BCE after a period of plainware production. That is a claim about a material practice. It does not establish the end of settlement or the disappearance of island communities, and it cannot be used as a uniform Pacific boundary.

orientations.perspectives: Objects preserve selected activities and deposits. Neither a museum classification nor the absence of later pottery gives a full account of how people identified themselves.
orientations.scope: Separate mainland and island comparisons, with no contact inferred between them. Later Phú Chánh and Luy Lâu evidence is not moved into the 300 BCE snapshot; it remains available in the dossier with its own dates.

activity.prompt: Rewrite “pottery stops, so the people vanished” using the evidence and one unanswered question.
activity.response: The study dates a change or end in ceramic manufacture. Ask what other settlement, food or material evidence could establish later community life; the pottery sequence alone cannot answer that question.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE falls within the broad Đông Sơn-associated frame. Individual drums and deposits still need their own dates. In Tonga it is later than the study’s proposed end of pottery manufacture; that material boundary does not demonstrate that island communities ended.
